learning_goal: Trace the sciatic nerve from the greater sciatic foramen to the popliteal fossa naming what it lies on at every step, mark its course on a patient, say what each of its two divisions supplies, and work out from a foot drop or a flail foot where the nerve has been damaged.

terms: midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter
no branch in the gluteal region

structures.name: right piriformis
structures.label: Piriformis
structures.narration: The one muscle you must find first. It comes out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and fills it, leaving a gap above and a gap below. The sciatic nerve uses the gap below. Everything else in the buttock is described as above piriformis or below piriformis.

structures.name: right gemellus superior
structures.label: Gemellus superior
structures.narration: The first thing the nerve lies on after it leaves the pelvis. From the ischial spine.

structures.name: right obturator internus
structures.label: Obturator internus
structures.narration: Its tendon turns a right angle through the lesser sciatic notch and comes out between the two twins. The nerve crosses that tendon second.

structures.name: right gemellus inferior
structures.label: Gemellus inferior
structures.narration: The lower twin. Third in the sequence.

structures.name: right quadratus femoris
structures.label: Quadratus femoris
terms: the nerve lies on quadratus femoris
structures.narration: The last and the largest bed. The sciatic nerve lies flat on quadratus femoris as it leaves the buttock, and that is the level at which it is midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter.

structures.name: right gluteus maximus
structures.label: Gluteus maximus
structures.narration: The roof. The whole gluteal course of the nerve is hidden under this one muscle, which is why nothing in this region can be felt and why a needle in the wrong quadrant reaches the nerve without warning.

structures.name: right gluteus medius
structures.label: Gluteus medius
structures.narration: Well above and lateral to the nerve. That is the whole reason an intramuscular injection is aimed at the upper outer quadrant and nowhere else.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: Three points on this bone fix the nerve: the greater sciatic notch it comes through, the ischial spine it passes below, and the ischial tuberosity that is one end of its surface marking. The acetabulum matters too — the nerve lies directly behind the hip joint.

structures.name: sacrum
structures.label: Sacrum
structures.narration: The roots come out of the front of this bone. The sacral plexus lies on piriformis inside the pelvis, and the nerve it forms leaves through the foramen bounded by the sacrum, the sacrotuberous ligament and the greater sciatic notch.

structures.name: right femur
structures.label: Femur
structures.narration: The greater trochanter is the landmark you can feel and the other end of the surface marking. The head of the femur is just in front of the nerve — a posterior dislocation drives it backwards into the nerve, which is why every dislocated hip is tested for foot drop before anything else is done.

structures.name: right fibula
structures.label: Fibula
structures.narration: The neck of this bone is the most dangerous point in the lower limb. The common fibular division winds round it under nothing but skin, so a tight plaster, a badly placed strap or a night on a hard edge produces a foot drop.

structures.label: Ischial tuberosity
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT point where semitendinosus (FMA22358, gap 0.39 mm) and the long head of biceps femoris (FMA45888, 0.49 mm) meet the hip bone — two witnesses 26.4 mm apart on a 207.9 mm bone (12.7%). Adductor magnus (FMA22459) was tried as a third witness and REJECTED: it scatters the set over 67.7 mm and the tool refused to emit, because that muscle also contacts the ischiopubic ramus far from the tuberosity. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --contact FMA22358,FMA45888
terms: midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter
structures.narration: What you sit on, and the medial end of the surface marking. The hamstrings arise here, and the nerve passes down just lateral to it.

structures.label: Ischial spine
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT point between the hip bone and gemellus superior (FMA22334), gap 0.05 mm — one witness, but gemellus superior arises from the ischial spine and from nowhere else, so the contact IS the spine. It sits 0.25 of the bone's height above the ischial tuberosity anchor (w 0.316 vs 0.066), which is the correct separation. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --contact FMA22334
structures.narration: The point that divides the greater sciatic foramen above from the lesser below. The nerve leaves above this level, through the greater foramen. Below it, through the lesser foramen, the tendon of obturator internus comes out — and the internal pudendal vessels and nerve go back in beside it.

structures.label: Posterior superior iliac spine
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the most POSTERIOR point of the upper quarter of the hip bone (extreme +y within z:0.75–1.0), 90.3 mm from the surface centroid. The PSIS is defined by position rather than by an attachment, so no contact measurement applies. It lands at v=0.998 — the back edge of the bone — which is what the definition asks for. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA16586 --extreme +y --slab z:0.75,1.0
terms: surface marking of the sciatic nerve
structures.narration: The skin dimple at the top of the buttock. The upper end of the surface marking starts midway between this point and the ischial tuberosity.

structures.label: Greater trochanter
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT point where gluteus medius (FMA22330, gap 0.13 mm), gluteus minimus (FMA22332, 0.57 mm) and piriformis (FMA22340, 0.11 mm) converge on the femur — three witnesses over 20.4 mm of a 440.2 mm bone (4.6%). Identical to the anchor of the same name in gross__gluteal-region-hip-joint__proximal-femur, deliberately: a student reads the two scenes consecutively and the landmark must not move between them. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA24474 --contact FMA22330,FMA22332,FMA22340
terms: midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter
structures.narration: The lateral end of the surface marking, and the only one of the three points you can feel through the buttock without pressing hard.

structures.label: Neck of the fibula
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the CONTACT point where fibularis longus (FMA22552, gap 0.17 mm) and extensor digitorum longus (FMA22548, 0.29 mm) meet the fibula — two witnesses 28.3 mm apart on a 351 mm bone (8.1%). Both arise from the head and upper shaft, so the mean lies just below the head: the tip of the fibula measures at w=1.000 (extreme +z) and this point is 27.7 mm below it, which is the level at which the common fibular nerve crosses. READ AS: a measured point on the upper fibula at neck level, not a measured neck — a neck is a narrowest cross-section, which is neither of this tool's two definitions. tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA24480 --contact FMA22552,FMA22548
structures.narration: The most dangerous 3 cm in the lower limb. The nerve is against bone here with nothing over it but skin.

structures.name: long head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — long head
structures.narration: The only muscle that crosses the nerve. It runs down and laterally over it, so in the thigh the nerve is deep to this head and lateral to the other two hamstrings. Tibial division.

structures.name: right semitendinosus
structures.label: Semitendinosus
structures.narration: Tibial division, like every hamstring except one.

structures.name: right semimembranosus
structures.label: Semimembranosus
structures.narration: Tibial division. Together with semitendinosus it forms the medial boundary of the popliteal fossa, where the nerve divides.

structures.name: right adductor magnus
structures.label: Adductor magnus — hamstring part
structures.narration: The nerve lies on the back of this muscle all the way down the thigh. Its ischial part is a hamstring and takes the tibial division; the rest of the muscle is obturator. One muscle, two nerves — a favourite question.

structures.name: medial head of right gastrocnemius
structures.label: Gastrocnemius — medial head
structures.narration: Below the knee the tibial nerve takes the whole back of the leg. Lose it and the patient cannot stand on tiptoe and the ankle jerk is gone.

structures.name: right soleus
structures.label: Soleus
structures.narration: Tibial nerve. The nerve passes under the tendinous arch of this muscle to reach the deep back of the leg.

structures.name: right tibialis posterior
structures.label: Tibialis posterior
structures.narration: Tibial nerve. It inverts the foot, so inversion is lost in a tibial lesion and preserved in a fibular one — that single movement separates the two.

structures.name: right flexor digitorum longus
structures.label: Flexor digitorum longus
structures.narration: Tibial nerve. The tibial division also takes every small muscle of the sole, and all the sensation there.

structures.name: short head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — short head
terms: the only muscle above the knee
structures.narration: The exception that examiners love. Every other hamstring is tibial; this one head is the only muscle the common fibular division supplies above the knee.

structures.name: right tibialis anterior
structures.label: Tibialis anterior
structures.narration: The muscle that lifts the front of the foot. Deep fibular nerve. When this is paralysed the toes catch on the ground and the patient lifts the knee high to clear them.

structures.name: right extensor digitorum longus
structures.label: Extensor digitorum longus
structures.narration: Deep fibular nerve, anterior compartment. Extends the toes as the foot is lifted.

structures.name: right extensor hallucis longus
structures.label: Extensor hallucis longus
structures.narration: Deep fibular nerve. Ask the patient to pull the big toe up against your finger — that is the cleanest test of L5 in the whole examination.

structures.name: right fibularis longus
structures.label: Fibularis longus
structures.narration: Superficial fibular nerve, lateral compartment. It everts the foot. Eversion is lost in a common fibular lesion and kept in a tibial one.

structures.name: right fibularis brevis
structures.label: Fibularis brevis
structures.narration: The other evertor, on the same nerve.

views.title: Where it comes out
views.narration: The sciatic nerve is formed inside the pelvis from L4, L5, S1, S2 and S3 and leaves through the greater sciatic foramen. Piriformis fills that foramen, and the nerve comes out below its lower border. That is the arrangement in about nine people in ten. In the rest the common fibular part pierces the muscle or passes above it, and those are the legs that ache when the muscle is tight.

views.title: Take the roof off
views.narration: Gluteus maximus is the lid. Lift it and the nerve is there, lying in fat on a floor of small muscles. Nothing in the gluteal region can be palpated, and the nerve gives off no branch at all while it is here — it is simply passing through.

views.title: What it lies on, in order
views.narration: The path traced here is the nerve itself. Learn the beds in order: gemellus superior, the tendon of obturator internus, gemellus inferior, then quadratus femoris. Recite that list in a viva and you have described the gluteal course exactly. Behind it lies only gluteus maximus; in front of it lies the capsule of the hip joint.

views.title: Mark it on a patient
views.narration: Three bony points give you the line, and all three are marked on the bones here — measured on the meshes, not placed by eye. Start midway between the posterior superior iliac spine and the ischial tuberosity. Curve laterally and downwards to a point midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. Then run straight down the middle of the back of the thigh to the top of the diamond behind the knee. Every clinical fact about this nerve hangs on that line.

views.title: Down the back of the thigh
views.narration: In the thigh the nerve lies on the back of adductor magnus with the hamstrings around it. Only one muscle crosses it: the long head of biceps femoris, running down and out over the top of it. Its branches to the hamstrings come off the medial side, which is why a surgeon works from the lateral side of the nerve.

views.title: Two nerves in one sheath
views.narration: The sciatic nerve is not one nerve. It is a tibial nerve and a common fibular nerve bound in a common sheath, and they separate at the top of the popliteal fossa. Lit on one side is everything tibial: all the hamstrings except one head, the hamstring part of adductor magnus, the whole back of the leg and the whole sole. Lit on the other is everything common fibular: the short head of biceps femoris, then the front and the side of the leg. Learn the division and you never have to learn a lesion.

views.title: The one head that breaks the rule
views.narration: One muscle, two heads, two different nerves. The long head is tibial like the rest of the hamstrings. The short head is common fibular, and it is the only muscle that division supplies above the knee. Because of it, a common fibular lesion high in the thigh weakens knee flexion very slightly, while a lesion at the fibula does not touch the thigh at all.

views.title: Foot drop at the neck of the fibula
views.narration: The common fibular nerve leaves the fossa along the tendon of biceps femoris, then winds round the neck of the fibula with nothing over it but skin. It is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb. The result is a foot drop: no dorsiflexion, no eversion, and a patch of numbness over the front and outer side of the leg and the top of the foot. The patient lifts the knee high and slaps the foot down. Inversion still works, because tibialis posterior is tibial.

views.title: The whole nerve cut
views.narration: A complete lesion in the buttock paralyses everything lit here. The hamstrings go, so knee flexion is weak, though gracilis and sartorius still bend it a little. Every muscle below the knee goes, so the foot is flail. Sensation is lost below the knee everywhere except a strip down the medial side, which belongs to the saphenous nerve from the femoral. The knee jerk is normal and the ankle jerk is absent — that pair localises the injury on its own.

views.title: How it gets damaged
views.narration: Three ways, and all three are examined. A needle in the wrong quadrant of the buttock — inject only into the upper outer quadrant, into gluteus medius, well clear of the nerve. A posterior dislocation of the hip, where the head of the femur is driven back onto the nerve. And surgery on the hip. Test dorsiflexion in every one of these patients before and after, and write down what you found.

views.title: Sciatica is not a sciatic nerve lesion
views.narration: Sciatica is pain down the back of the leg, and the usual cause is a prolapsed disc pressing a nerve root at L5 or S1, far above anything shown in the buttock. The trunk itself is rarely the problem. Piriformis syndrome is the exception worth knowing: a tight or overworked piriformis squeezing the nerve at the foramen, giving buttock pain that is worse on sitting. A straight leg raise reproduces the pain in both, so the history and the level of the sensory loss decide.

views.title: How deep is it
views.narration: Drag the cut and count the layers a needle passes: skin, a thick pad of fat, gluteus maximus, then the loose fat that holds the nerve and the gluteal vessels, then the short rotators on the back of the hip joint. The nerve sits in that fourth layer, about as wide as your little finger. In a large adult it can be five centimetres or more from the surface, and there is no warning on the way down.

gaps: The subject of this scene has no model. There is no nerve of the lower limb in the catalog — of 934 entries the only nerves are the right and left optic nerves — so the sciatic nerve is authored as a traced concept path across the muscles it lies on, and its two divisions are taught by lighting the muscles they supply. Every other structure named here resolves to a real model, and the teaching is the standard one: in the gluteal region the nerve has no branches and no palpable landmark, so it is located entirely by what it crosses.

Status is 'candidate', not 'ready'. The scene passes the gate and renders, but the structure the curriculum asked for is present only as a concept path, and a human should decide whether a trace over the correct beds is enough to call the entry taught. Promote to 'ready' on that decision, or when a sciatic nerve model exists and the traces are re-authored against it.

3d_anatomy is used and 'diagram' is recorded in deferred_modes. A drawn diagram would show the nerve itself, the root values and the sensory map far better than a trace does; the 3D scene is stronger on the relations, the depth and the injection anatomy. Ideally the topic ends up with both.

No ligament of the pelvis is modelled. The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments complete the greater sciatic foramen the nerve leaves through, and the sacrospinous ligament separates it from the lesser sciatic foramen. Both are narrated only.

The ischial spine, the ischial tuberosity, the posterior superior iliac spine, the greater trochanter and the neck of the fibula are sub-features of whole-bone models. All five are now MEASURED landmark anchors, each carrying its measurement in calibrated_by and each status 'needs-review', so beat 4 marks the nerve on a patient against points on the bone rather than by lighting whole bones. The greater trochanter anchor is the same coordinate as in the proximal femur scene by design. The neck of the fibula is the weakest of the five and says so in its own calibrated_by: it is a measured point at neck level, derived from where fibularis longus and extensor digitorum longus arise, not a measured neck.

The GREATER SCIATIC NOTCH was NOT authored as an anchor and no later run should try. It is a concavity — a notch is defined by the absence of bone — so the nearest-contact definition returns the muscle lying across it and the extreme definition returns the rim on either side. Neither is the notch. It stays named on the hip bone in beat 1 and in the hip_bone narration.

The sensory territory of the nerve cannot be shown. The only skin in the catalog is FMA7163, a single whole-body mesh with no regional divisions, so a dermatome patch cannot be lit on it and beats 8 and 9 describe the numb areas instead. The saphenous strip on the medial side of the leg, which is the exception that proves the lesion is sciatic and not spinal, is narration only.
The intrinsic muscles of the sole are not modelled individually here, so the tibial division's hand-like control of the foot is represented by flexor digitorum longus and named in narration.

The artery to the sciatic nerve, from the inferior gluteal artery, is named but not shown. No gluteal vessel exists as a model — that gap belongs to the Gluteal vessels entry, which is authored separately and which this scene does not claim to cover.
This scene does not cover Gluteus maximus, Hip joint or Proximal femur. Those muscles and bones appear only as the roof, the floor and the frame that fix the nerve's position.
